title: Scheduled Task Created by Non-Admin
summary: Scheduled task created by a non-administrative account detection identifies task registration activity where the creating account is an ordinary user or a service identity that has no legitimate business reason to establish persistence, autostart or system level execution on the host. The behaviour matters because scheduled tasks are one of the most reliable and least disruptive persistence mechanisms on Windows: they survive reboot, they can run under a privileged context through stored credentials, and they are frequently used for recurring beaconing, dropper staging and privilege escalation through writable task definitions. The telemetry required is process creation for the task scheduling utility along with its command line, scheduled task operational events recording task name, creating account, action to execute and the principal the task runs as, and process creation correlated to the task engine so that the executed child process can be attributed back to the task definition. The signal survives common evasion because registration is an unavoidable step: an operator may use the command line tool, a scripting interface, a management API or a signed binary proxy, but all of these result in a task definition written to the task store, and the resulting execution appears as a child of the task scheduling service. Attackers who avoid the task store by using alternative autostart locations still remove themselves from this detection's scope, which is why it belongs in a family of autostart detections rather than standing alone. The detection breaks down in practice because non-administrative users in many organisations legitimately create their own logon tasks, software installers register per-user update tasks constantly, and cloud connected productivity and collaboration clients rebuild their scheduled entries after every upgrade. Task names are also attacker-controlled, so name-based matching produces both false positives and false negatives. The workable approach is to score on the creating account's privilege relative to the task principal, the writability of the executable path referenced, and the relationship between task creation and surrounding process activity, rather than on the existence of the task alone.
objectives: Explain why the relationship between the creating account and the task principal matters more than the task name.
Query task registration telemetry to extract the executing path, the run-as principal and the trigger configuration.
Identify task definitions that reference user-writable directories, script interpreters or remote content.
Baseline legitimate per-user updater tasks from productivity and collaboration software in your environment.
Correlate task execution with the originating process tree to attribute running payloads back to the schedule.
Recommend hardening measures that restrict non-administrative task creation without breaking vendor updaters.
dataSources: Windows Security event 4698 scheduled task creation including task name, content and creating subject
Process creation telemetry for the task registration utility with full command line
Task Scheduler operational log entries recording task registration and execution start
Windows Security event 4688 process creation capturing the task engine spawning the configured action
Account group membership data identifying whether the creating account holds administrative rights
logic: Alert when a task registration event is attributed to an account that does not hold administrative rights, or when the task principal is more privileged than the creating account, and enrich the alert with the executable or script path the task will run. Add severity when the referenced path is inside a user profile, temporary directory, or other location writable by non-administrators, when the action invokes a scripting interpreter or downloads remote content, and when the task is configured to run at logon or on a short repeating interval. Reduce severity for tasks created by known software updaters with signed binaries in program directories and a stable name pattern, and correlate the alert with the process that the task engine actually launched so that running payloads can be attributed and collected.
pseudoQuery:
title: Scheduled Task Registered By Non-Administrative Account
id: det-scheduled-task-non-admin
status: training
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security
detection:
  task_registered:
    EventID: 4698
  non_admin_creator:
    SubjectUserName|endswith:
      - '$'
    # creator is not a member of the local administrators group
  suspicious_action:
    TaskContent|contains:
      - 'powershell'
      - 'cmd.exe /c'
      - 'wscript'
      - 'mshta'
      - 'rundll32'
      - '\\AppData\\'
      - '\\Temp\\'
      - '\\Users\\Public\\'
  condition: task_registered and (non_admin_creator or suspicious_action)
fields:
  - TaskName
  - SubjectUserName
  - TaskContent
  - Computer
level: high
falsePositives: Cloud synchronisation and collaboration clients that register per-user update or maintenance tasks
Software installers and updaters running in user context that recreate their scheduled entries after upgrade
Administrative scripts running under a delegated service account that is not in the local administrators group
Endpoint management agents that register inventory or compliance tasks on behalf of a system service
Developer tooling that schedules builds, test runs or cleanup jobs under the interactive user account
tuningNotes: Build the exclusion set from the pair of task name pattern and executable path rather than from the task name alone, because attacker chosen names frequently imitate vendor naming conventions. Where the deployment supports it, resolve the creator's effective group membership at alert time instead of relying on the account name suffix, since delegated and just-in-time administrative accounts do not follow naming rules. Keep severity low, but do not discard, tasks whose action references a signed binary in a protected program directory; instead route them to a weekly review so that a compromised updater change is still visible. Supplement the rule with detection of task modification and deletion events, since operators increasingly modify an existing benign task instead of creating a new one, and that behaviour is invisible to a creation-only rule.

beginner.definition: A scheduled task is an instruction Windows runs later, either once or on a repeating timetable. An administrative account is one with broad control over a computer. This detection flags tasks created by ordinary accounts. It also flags tasks set to run as a more powerful account than their creator.
beginner.whyItMatters: Tasks are a favourite way to stay on a machine, because they survive a restart. They also look like ordinary system behaviour. An attacker can register one quietly, then let Windows relaunch their program every hour or at each sign-in. Many organisations let normal users create tasks. This activity therefore sits inside allowed behaviour, so it needs its own alert.
howItWorks: Windows writes an audit record whenever a new scheduled task is registered.
That record names the task, the account that created it and the command the task will run.
It also shows which account the task runs as, which may be more powerful than the creator.
The detection compares the two accounts and checks whether the creator normally holds admin rights.
It also looks at the target path, because files in user folders and temporary areas are common hiding places.
High-risk tasks are correlated with what the task actually launched later, so running code can be traced.
beginner.example: Think of an apartment building where any tenant may leave a written instruction at the front desk. One tenant leaves a note for the maintenance crew. It asks them to unlock the manager's office at two in the morning. The crew is allowed to do it and the tenant is allowed to leave notes. Nothing about either action looks broken. Yet the combination is wrong, and the manager should ask why.
takeaways: Scheduled tasks are a durable way to stay on a machine across restarts.
Compare who created the task with the account it will run as.
Judge a task by its target path and command, not by its name.
